keep: He kept the engines and gave his partner everything else. When the engines went against him, he stayed as president, and left when his partner did.
lede: He gave Takeo Fujisawa the sales, the money and every bank, and kept only the engineering. When Fujisawa retired in 1973, he went too: "I'm only here as president because of Takeo Fujisawa."
copy: Soichiro Honda was born in 1906 into a blacksmith's family that later sold bicycles. At fifteen he answered an advertisement in his father's trade magazine and went to Tokyo as a live-in apprentice at Art Shokai, owned by Ikuzo Sakakibara. At twenty-one he opened its branch in Hamamatsu, where he was called the "Edison of Hamamatsu." In 1936 he founded Tokai Seiki to make piston rings, and they did not work: Toyota, by its own media site's account, ordered 30,000 and sent back 47 of the first 50 samples. At thirty he began auditing night classes at the Hamamatsu Technical High School to learn metallurgy, and he went on to hold 28 patents. The company grew to about 2,000 people, came under government control in 1941, and on the Munitions Ministry's instruction Toyota took a 40 per cent stake, after which Honda stepped down as president. An air raid destroyed the factory, and an earthquake followed. He sold his shares to Toyota for ¥450,000 and spent about a year making homemade liquor.

On 1 September 1946 he set up the Honda Technical Research Institute and fitted bicycles with about 500 small army generator engines, built to power wireless radios. Honda Motor Co. was founded on 24 September 1948 with one million yen. In August 1949, the month the Dream D-Type came out, Hiroshi Takeshima introduced him to Takeo Fujisawa; Honda was 42, Fujisawa 38. The company's own history says Honda entrusted Fujisawa with sales, finance and organisation, everything except technology, and with all its banking. The Super Cub went on sale in August 1958, and its series passed 100 million in October 2017. American Honda began selling in September 1959 with eight staff, on $250,000 the Ministry of Finance allowed after refusing a million, and sold 170 machines that year. The big motorcycles were the plan, and they broke. "We had no choice," Kawashima, of American Honda, told Richard Pascale. "We let the 50cc bikes move."

In engines he was stubborn, and once wrong. He wanted them air-cooled: "The water for the water-cooling is ultimately cooled by the air. Then, why not use air-cooling to begin with?" The air-cooled H1300 went on sale in May 1969 and did not sell as the company expected, while engineers under Tadashi Kume built a water-cooled engine without telling him. Fujisawa asked whether he wanted to stay with Honda as president or as an engineer. "I will stay as president." The CVCC engine, announced in February 1971, passed the Environmental Protection Agency's tests for the 1975 standard at Ann Arbor in December 1972. In his resignation speech he said of a young engineer, "His argument opened up my eyes and truly inspired me." He died on 5 August 1991, aged 84.

bio.t: Honda Motor: The Men, the Management, the Machines
bio.why: The partnership is the story, and this book, translated from the Japanese, covers both men. Sol Sanders's Honda: The Man and His Machines is the better-known life. Honda's own online history, 75 Years of History, is the source of most of the words in quotation marks here.

contested: Whether Honda planned America, and what "first" means. The Boston Consulting Group's report of 1975, Strategy Alternatives for the British Motorcycle Industry, described a deliberate entry from the bottom of the market, driven by scale. Richard Pascale, interviewing Honda's men in America for the California Management Review in 1984, found the opposite: the big bikes were the plan, and the Super Cub carried the business when they failed. In a forum in the same journal in 1996, Michael Goold, a co-author of the BCG report, answered that it was written for an industry in crisis and was "much more valid" for that purpose; Henry Mintzberg replied that it "erred in its inferences" and misled any manager who read it; Richard Rumelt said Pascale's story only covers the first entry. Pascale's own dates are loose against the company's. He also says "You meet the nicest people on a Honda" began as a UCLA student's class assignment that Grey Advertising bought; Honda credits Grey. The CVCC engine passed the 1975 standard in a Nissan weighted with sandbags, the deadline was then postponed, and Honda's own Civic first failed certification before passing in November 1974. Tokai Seiki's founding is 1936 in Honda's history and 1937 elsewhere. And the story that he refused to let his sons into the company is told widely but not in anything this house has opened, so it is not repeated here.
